items.title: Identifying Convergent or Divergent Integrals With Unbounded Limits

sections.normalized_html:
Consider the function [MATH: f(x) = e^{-x}.] Which of the following statements are true?

  1. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_0^\infty f(x) \, \textrm dx] is convergent

  2. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^0 f(x) \, \textrm dx] is divergent

  3. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x) \, \textrm dx] is divergent
sections.readable_text:
Consider the function [MATH: f(x) = e^{-x}.] Which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_0^\infty f(x) \, \textrm dx] is convergent
2. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^0 f(x) \, \textrm dx] is divergent
3. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x) \, \textrm dx] is divergent

sections.normalized_html:
Suppose we have an improper integral in which both the left and right endpoints are unbounded:

[MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x]

If the integrand [MATH: f(x)] is continuous on [MATH: (-\infty, \infty),] then we can break the integral up into two improper integrals, each with a single unbounded endpoint:

[MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = \int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x]

Then, we can compute each of the two integrals separately and combine their results.

Watch out! If either of the two integrals on the right-hand side is divergent, then the integral on the left-hand side is also divergent.

With that in mind, let's examine our integrals.

  • Computing the integral in statement I, we get [MATH: \eqalign{ \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-x}\, \textrm{d}x &= \lim_{a \to \infty} \int_{0}^{a} e^{-x}\, \textrm{d}x \ &= \lim_{a \to \infty} \left[-e^{-x}\right]_0^a\ &= -\lim_{a \to \infty} \left({e^{-a}}-1\right)\ &= 1. }] So the integral converges, and statement I is true.

  • Computing the integral in statement II, we get [MATH: ∫_{− ∞}^{0}e^{− x}dx|= lim_(a → − ∞)∫_{a}^{0}e^{− x}dx; = lim_(a → − ∞)[− e^{− x}]_{a}^{0}; = lim_(a → − ∞)(e^{− a} − 1); = + ∞.] So the integral diverges, and statement II is true.

  • The integral in statement III can be expressed as [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x) \, \textrm dx= \int_{-\infty}^0 f(x) \, \textrm dx + \int_0^\infty f(x) \, \textrm dx.] However, the first integral on the right-hand side is divergent. Therefore, the integral on the left-hand side is also divergent, and statement III is true.

In conclusion, statements I, II, and III are all true.

Suppose we have an improper integral in which both the left and right endpoints are unbounded:

[MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x]

If the integrand [MATH: f(x)] is continuous on [MATH: (-\infty, \infty),] then we can break the integral up into two improper integrals, each with a single unbounded endpoint:

[MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = \int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x]

Then, we can compute each of the two integrals separately and combine their results.

Watch out! If either of the two integrals on the right-hand side is divergent, then the integral on the left-hand side is also divergent.

With that in mind, let's examine our integrals.

- Computing the integral in statement I, we get
[MATH: \eqalign{
\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-x}\, \textrm{d}x
&= \lim_{a \to \infty} \int_{0}^{a} e^{-x}\, \textrm{d}x \
&= \lim_{a \to \infty} \left[-e^{-x}\right]_0^a\
&= -\lim_{a \to \infty} \left({e^{-a}}-1\right)\
&= 1.
}]
So the integral converges, and statement I is true.
- Computing the integral in statement II, we get
[MATH: ∫_{− ∞}^{0}e^{− x}dx|= lim_(a → − ∞)∫_{a}^{0}e^{− x}dx; = lim_(a → − ∞)[− e^{− x}]_{a}^{0}; = lim_(a → − ∞)(e^{− a} − 1); = + ∞.]
So the integral diverges, and statement II is true.
- The integral in statement III can be expressed as
[MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x) \, \textrm dx= \int_{-\infty}^0 f(x) \, \textrm dx + \int_0^\infty f(x) \, \textrm dx.]
However, the first integral on the right-hand side is divergent. Therefore, the integral on the left-hand side is also divergent, and statement III is true.

In conclusion, statements I, II, and III are all true.

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Suppose we have an improper integral in which both the left and right endpoints are unbounded:

[MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x]

With that in mind, let's examine our integrals.

- Computing the integral in statement I, we get
[MATH: \eqalign{
\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-x}\, \textrm{d}x
&= \lim_{a \to \infty} \int_{0}^{a} e^{-x}\, \textrm{d}x \
&= \lim_{a \to \infty} \left[-e^{-x}\right]_0^a\
&= -\lim_{a \to \infty} \left({e^{-a}}-1\right)\
&= 1.
}]
So the integral converges, and statement I is true.
- Computing the integral in statement II, we get
[MATH: ∫_{− ∞}^{0}e^{− x}dx|= lim_(a → − ∞)∫_{a}^{0}e^{− x}dx; = lim_(a → − ∞)[− e^{− x}]_{a}^{0}; = lim_(a → − ∞)(e^{− a} − 1); = + ∞.]
So the integral diverges, and statement II is true.
- The integral in statement III can be expressed as
[MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x) \, \textrm dx= \int_{-\infty}^0 f(x) \, \textrm dx + \int_0^\infty f(x) \, \textrm dx.]
However, the first integral on the right-hand side is divergent. Therefore, the integral on the left-hand side is also divergent, and statement III is true.

In conclusion, statements I, II, and III are all true.

items.title: Improper Integrals of Even and Odd Functions

sections.normalized_html: Computing the definite integral of a function over the entire real line requires us to break the integral into two parts and separately evaluate each one.

sections.normalized_html: Evaluating two improper integrals can be quite time-consuming. However, we can shorten the process if we see that [MATH: f(x)] is an even or odd function.
sections.readable_text: Evaluating two improper integrals can be quite time-consuming. However, we can shorten the process if we see that [MATH: f(x)] is an even or odd function.

sections.normalized_html:
• Recall that [MATH: f(x)] is an even function if [MATH: f(-x) = f(x).] Even functions are symmetrical about the [MATH: y]-axis. Therefore, if [MATH: f(x)] is even, we have [MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = \int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x,] provided that the integrals are convergent. Moreover, if [MATH: f(x)] is even and the above integrals are convergent, then [MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = 2\int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x.]

  • Recall that [MATH: f(x)] is an odd function if [MATH: f(-x) = -f(x).] Therefore, if [MATH: f(x)] is odd, we have [MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = -\int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x,] provided that the integrals are convergent. Moreover, if [MATH: f(x)] is odd and the above integrals are convergent, then [MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = 0.]

Evaluating two improper integrals can be quite time-consuming. However, we can shorten the process if we see that [MATH: f(x)] is an even or odd function.

[MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = -\int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x,]
provided that the integrals are convergent. Moreover, if [MATH: f(x)] is odd and the above integrals are convergent, then
[MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = 0.]

items.title: Calculating an Improper Integral With Unbounded Limits

sections.normalized_html:
We break up the integral as follows:

[MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \, \textrm{d}x = \int_{-\infty}^{0} \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \, \textrm{d}x.]

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get

[MATH: \eqalign{ \int_{-\infty}^0 \dfrac {1}{x^2+1} \,\textrm{d}x &= \lim_{a \to -\infty} \int_{a}^0 \dfrac {1}{x^2+1} \,\textrm{d}x\[5pt] & = \lim_{a \to -\infty}\left( \arctan (x) \Big|_a^0 \right) \[5pt] & = \lim_{a \to -\infty} \left[\arctan \left( 0 \right) - \arctan \left( a \right) \right] \[5pt] & = 0 - \lim_{a \to -\infty} \arctan \left( a \right) \[5pt] &= - \left(-\dfrac \pi 2 \right)\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\pi}{2}. }]

Now, notice that the integrand is an even function (i.e., it is symmetrical about the [MATH: y]-axis). This means that we can immediately deduce that

[MATH: \int_{0}^\infty \dfrac {1}{x^2+1} \,\textrm{d}x =\dfrac{\pi}{2}.]

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that [MATH: \eqalign{ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \, \textrm{d}x &= \int_{-\infty}^{0} \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt] &=\dfrac{\pi}{2}+ \dfrac{\pi}{2}\[5pt] &= \pi.}]

&= \lim_{a \to -\infty} \int_{a}^0 \dfrac {1}{x^2+1} \,\textrm{d}x\[5pt]

& = \lim_{a \to -\infty}\left( \arctan (x) \Big|_a^0 \right) \[5pt]

& = \lim_{a \to -\infty} \left[\arctan \left( 0 \right) - \arctan \left( a \right) \right] \[5pt]

& = 0 - \lim_{a \to -\infty} \arctan \left( a \right) \[5pt]

&= - \left(-\dfrac \pi 2 \right)\[5pt]

& = \dfrac{\pi}{2}.

[MATH: \int_{0}^\infty \dfrac {1}{x^2+1} \,\textrm{d}x =\dfrac{\pi}{2}.]

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that
[MATH: \eqalign{
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \, \textrm{d}x &= \int_{-\infty}^{0} \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]

&=\dfrac{\pi}{2}+ \dfrac{\pi}{2}\[5pt]

&= \pi.}]

sections.normalized_html: Find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve [MATH: y = \dfrac{9}{1+4x^2}] and the [MATH: x]-axis.
sections.readable_text: Find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve [MATH: y = \dfrac{9}{1+4x^2}] and the [MATH: x]-axis.

sections.normalized_html:
Let's sketch a graph of the region.

In this case, we must calculate the improper integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \dfrac{9}{4x^2+1}\,\textrm{d}x.]

As usual, we break up the integral as follows: [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \dfrac{9}{4x^2+1}\,\textrm{d}x = \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{0} \dfrac{9}{4x^2+1}\,\textrm{d}x + \displaystyle \int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{9}{4x^2+1}\,\textrm{d}x]

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get [MATH: \eqalign{ \int_{-\infty}^0 \dfrac {9}{4x^2+1} \,\textrm{d}x & = 9\lim_{a \to -\infty}\left( \left[\dfrac{1}{2}\arctan \left(2x \right) \right]_a^0 \right) \[5pt] & = \dfrac{9}{2} \lim_{a \to -\infty} \left[\arctan \left( 0 \right) - \arctan \left( 2a \right) \right] \[5pt] & = 0 - \dfrac{9}{2}\lim_{a \to -\infty} \arctan \left( 2a \right) \[5pt] & = -\dfrac{9}{2} \left(-\dfrac \pi 2 \right)\[5pt] & = \dfrac{9\pi}{4}. }]

Now, notice that the integrand is an even function. Therefore, we can immediately deduce that

[MATH: \displaystyle \int_{0}^\infty\dfrac {9}{4x^2+1} \,\textrm{d}x = \dfrac{9\pi}{4}.]

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that [MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \dfrac{9}{4x^2+1}\,\textrm{d}x = \dfrac{9\pi}{4}+ \dfrac{9\pi}{4}= \dfrac{9\pi}{2} .]

So, the required area is equal to [MATH: \dfrac{9\pi}{2}] square units.

& = -\dfrac{9}{2} \left(-\dfrac \pi 2 \right)\[5pt]

[MATH: \displaystyle \int_{0}^\infty\dfrac {9}{4x^2+1} \,\textrm{d}x = \dfrac{9\pi}{4}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider an improper integral in which both the left and right endpoints are unbounded:

Content:
[MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x]

Content:
If the integrand [MATH: f(x)] is continuous on [MATH: (-\infty, \infty),] then we can break the integral up into two improper integrals, each with a single unbounded endpoint:

Content:
[MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = \int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x]

Content:
Then, we can compute each of the two integrals separately and combine their results.

Content:
Watch out! If either of the two integrals on the right-hand side is divergent, then the integral on the left-hand side is also divergent.

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Convergent or Divergent Integrals With Unbounded Limits

Example Prompt:
Consider the function [MATH: f(x) = e^{-x}.] Which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_0^\infty f(x) \, \textrm dx] is convergent
2. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^0 f(x) \, \textrm dx] is divergent
3. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x) \, \textrm dx] is divergent

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Suppose we have an improper integral in which both the left and right endpoints are unbounded:

[MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x]

If the integrand [MATH: f(x)] is continuous on [MATH: (-\infty, \infty),] then we can break the integral up into two improper integrals, each with a single unbounded endpoint:

[MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = \int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x]

Then, we can compute each of the two integrals separately and combine their results.

Watch out! If either of the two integrals on the right-hand side is divergent, then the integral on the left-hand side is also divergent.

With that in mind, let's examine our integrals.

- Computing the integral in statement I, we get
[MATH: \eqalign{
\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-x}\, \textrm{d}x
&= \lim_{a \to \infty} \int_{0}^{a} e^{-x}\, \textrm{d}x \
&= \lim_{a \to \infty} \left[-e^{-x}\right]_0^a\
&= -\lim_{a \to \infty} \left({e^{-a}}-1\right)\
&= 1.
}]
So the integral converges, and statement I is true.
- Computing the integral in statement II, we get
[MATH: ∫_{− ∞}^{0}e^{− x}dx|= lim_(a → − ∞)∫_{a}^{0}e^{− x}dx; = lim_(a → − ∞)[− e^{− x}]_{a}^{0}; = lim_(a → − ∞)(e^{− a} − 1); = + ∞.]
So the integral diverges, and statement II is true.
- The integral in statement III can be expressed as
[MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x) \, \textrm dx= \int_{-\infty}^0 f(x) \, \textrm dx + \int_0^\infty f(x) \, \textrm dx.]
However, the first integral on the right-hand side is divergent. Therefore, the integral on the left-hand side is also divergent, and statement III is true.

In conclusion, statements I, II, and III are all true.

Item 5 — Tutorial: Improper Integrals of Even and Odd Functions

Content:
Computing the definite integral of a function over the entire real line requires us to break the integral into two parts and separately evaluate each one.

Content:
[MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = \int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x]

Content:
Evaluating two improper integrals can be quite time-consuming. However, we can shorten the process if we see that [MATH: f(x)] is an even or odd function.

Content:
- Recall that [MATH: f(x)] is an even function if [MATH: f(-x) = f(x).] Even functions are symmetrical about the [MATH: y]-axis. Therefore, if [MATH: f(x)] is even, we have
[MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = \int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x,]
provided that the integrals are convergent. Moreover, if [MATH: f(x)] is even and the above integrals are convergent, then
[MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = 2\int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x.]
- Recall that [MATH: f(x)] is an odd function if [MATH: f(-x) = -f(x).] Therefore, if [MATH: f(x)] is odd, we have
[MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = -\int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x,]
provided that the integrals are convergent. Moreover, if [MATH: f(x)] is odd and the above integrals are convergent, then
[MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = 0.]

---

Item 6 — Example: Calculating an Improper Integral With Unbounded Limits

Example Prompt:
Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \, \textrm{d}x .]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We break up the integral as follows:

[MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \, \textrm{d}x = \int_{-\infty}^{0} \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \, \textrm{d}x.]

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get

[MATH: \eqalign{
\int_{-\infty}^0 \dfrac {1}{x^2+1} \,\textrm{d}x

&= \lim_{a \to -\infty} \int_{a}^0 \dfrac {1}{x^2+1} \,\textrm{d}x\[5pt]

& = \lim_{a \to -\infty}\left( \arctan (x) \Big|_a^0 \right) \[5pt]

& = \lim_{a \to -\infty} \left[\arctan \left( 0 \right) - \arctan \left( a \right) \right] \[5pt]

& = 0 - \lim_{a \to -\infty} \arctan \left( a \right) \[5pt]

&= - \left(-\dfrac \pi 2 \right)\[5pt]

& = \dfrac{\pi}{2}.
}]

Now, notice that the integrand is an even function (i.e., it is symmetrical about the [MATH: y]-axis). This means that we can immediately deduce that

[MATH: \int_{0}^\infty \dfrac {1}{x^2+1} \,\textrm{d}x =\dfrac{\pi}{2}.]

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that
[MATH: \eqalign{
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \, \textrm{d}x &= \int_{-\infty}^{0} \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]

&=\dfrac{\pi}{2}+ \dfrac{\pi}{2}\[5pt]

&= \pi.}]
